question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man with a decade-long history of ischemic cardiomyopathy complicated by episodes of pulmonary congestion (last outpatient echocardiogram three months earlier showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 30 %) and New York Heart Association class III baseline exertional tolerance arrived to the emergency department at 07:40 after vomiting two basinfuls of dark red, particle-laden fluid at home roughly ninety minutes prior to presentation. He explained that he had awakened with a sour, metallic taste, noted mild epigastric pressure that built over thirty minutes, then retched forcefully, producing what he called “old blood with some coffee-ground grit” but no bright red clots. He was able to remain seated at the kitchen table and walk independently to his neighbor’s car for transport. He denied seeing pitch-black, tarry, malodorous stools during the past week; his most recent bowel movement the previous evening was medium brown, soft, and flushed easily. There had been no change in urine color, no pruritus, and no yellowing of the eyes or skin. He has never been told that he has cirrhosis, hepatitis, or any other chronic liver condition, and prior laboratory panels have consistently shown normal hepatic function. He reported progressive ankle swelling over the last few days, orthopnea relieved by three pillows, and occasional paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea—symptoms that mirror his usual pattern when he inadvertently increases dietary sodium—but no chest pain, palpitations beyond his customary awareness of premature beats, cough, or fever. Daily medications include carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg every twelve hours, torsemide 40 mg each morning with potassium chloride 20 mEq, and low-dose aspirin 81 mg; he admitted that his cardiologist recently instructed him to stop non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, though he took ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for a flare of lumbar disc disease during the past five days. He has never been prescribed oral anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents other than aspirin, or corticosteroids. Surgical history is limited to open reduction of an ankle fracture two decades ago. His father died of congestive heart failure at 71, his mother of stroke at 74; there is no family history of peptic ulcer disease or bleeding diatheses. He stopped smoking ten years ago after a 35-pack-year habit and drinks a glass of wine on holidays but otherwise denies alcohol. Review of systems was negative for weight loss, night sweats, easy bruising, gingival bleeding, abdominal distention, or hematochezia. On arrival—before any intravenous access, antiemetics, acid suppression, vasoactive medication, crystalloid resuscitation, or transfusion were given—he sat upright on the stretcher, appeared pale and mildly diaphoretic, yet conversed in full sentences and was oriented to person, place, and time. Triage vitals obtained with an automated cuff documented a blood pressure of 107 / 66 mm Hg, a regular radial pulse of 103 beats per minute confirmed on the cardiac monitor, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oral temperature 37.0 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % while breathing ambient air. Capillary refill was nearly three seconds; jugular venous pulsation extended 9 cm above the sternal angle with the head of bed at 45°. Cardiac examination revealed a diffuse, laterally displaced apical impulse and an audible third heart sound without new murmurs; bibasilar crackles were faint but cleared after the patient sat forward. Peripheral pulses were 1-2 + bilaterally, and trace pitting edema was noted at both ankles. Lungs were otherwise clear. Abdominal inspection showed no distention or venous collaterals; palpation elicited moderate tenderness in the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly, and percussion suggested a liver span of 10 cm. Bowel sounds were brisk. The skin lacked spider angiomata, palmar erythema, or excoriations, and sclerae were anicteric. A focused neurologic survey demonstrated intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all extremities, and normal cerebellar finger-to-nose testing. Digital rectal examination produced a small smear of brown stool that turned the guaiac card dark blue within seconds but had no tarry quality. One 18-gauge peripheral catheter was placed for laboratory sampling only, after which the following results were available, all drawn prior to any therapeutic intervention: hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, hematocrit 37 %, mean corpuscular volume 91 fL, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 8.7 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 49 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.2 mg/dL), sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 95 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 32 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 29 U/L, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.09. A 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded concurrently showed sinus tachycardia at 104 bpm with Q-waves in the inferior leads consistent with old infarct and no acute ischemic changes. Upright chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly with mild pulmonary vascular congestion and no infiltrates; supine abdominal series revealed a nonspecific gas pattern without free air. The patient was placed NPO, a type and screen for cross-match was sent, continuous telemetry was initiated, and gastroenterology consultation was requested for urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy to localize and treat the suspected upper gastrointestinal source of bleeding in the context of his chronic cardiomyopathy.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses pretreatment laboratory values, vital signs, symptoms, and comorbidities.
- BUN 49 mg/dL corresponds to urea 17.5 mmol/L (10 to <25): 4 points.
- Hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL in a man (12 to <13): 1 point.
- Systolic BP 107 mm Hg (100–109): 1 point.
- Pulse 103/min (≥100): 1 point.
- Melena: 0 points. The stool is brown, not tarry; a positive guaiac test is not melena.
- Syncope: none reported, 0 points.
- Hepatic disease: none, 0 points.
- Heart failure: symptomatic ischemic cardiomyopathy with EF 30%, 2 points.
Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 9.
Final answer: 9
